en: Preface to the Re-edited Sequence of the Five Ranks of Caodong, Presented to the Chief Preceptor Shoucheng by Xuecen. Consider this carefully:
the lineage of Shitou originates from Caoxi. It has been nourished through four generations until it reached Dongshan; its current flow—

It began with greatness; filling every basin until it overflowed, it proceeded with order and without confusion. Since the Great Master passed away, five generations have elapsed until we reach Dayang.

The methods of his spiritual machinery had not yet fully integrated, and this Way was desolate. It was thanks to the opening of the Ciji Pagoda that extraordinary sprouts emerged from between the weeds.

He stirred the turbid waters to flow freely toward Huai and Shu, thereby securing the entrustment of a thread suspended in mid-air; he caused the fragrance to spread to Xiang and Ying, able to turn back what had already been overturned.
As the great tide ebbed, the waves surged over Tongnyeong and swirled at Sasin; the currents dried up the earth and washed away the heavens in boundless turbulence.
Thus, those that subsequently reached海东 (Haidong) were but its lingering foam.
For this reason, among the followers of the school, few have attained its pure and complete essence. Nevertheless, there were those such as Geumjang of Silla, and Inyeom, Cheonghu, Ungju, and Susimi.

Yan Wuwei, Wei Yan, Kouxue, Xufeng, Zhan Daling, Qingyuan, Wolong, Hailong, Ruiyan, and Jiyan—these twenty or so venerable elders currently appearing in the records are those who are purest of the pure.
Each has attained a profound and overflowing realization, returning to the source as if returning to Lu and transforming through that return.
Thus, it is they who have enabled the subtle harmony of the Middle Way to flourish throughout the land of Qingqiu. As for their...

This tradition has existed for a long time. Yet, in recent times, descendants have laid bare their five [errors]: they are as inflexible as one who fixes a peg to a harp string or marks a boat’s position after it has sailed away.

This has caused the state of the One Flavor (yīwèi) to become exceedingly degenerate. Some people confront this with superficial "stem-grass Chan" (*gēngcǎo chán*), claiming it involves conceptual thought and placing it beyond the threshold of true practice;

others retreat, gazing toward the distant shore from within the vast, chaotic depths. Alas! The "Guangling San" melody is nearly extinct. Is it not said that when two blades clash, one must strike decisively?

Lightning and fire are difficult to pursue; once movement begins, one falls into habitual patterns and stumbles, lingering in hesitation. How often has this misled people, causing them to lose their true intent and shed blood from their fingers in shame?
There are clear proofs of this: the resentful wife who slandered her husband to the point that he drowned, and the old friend whose milk became poison. These cases serve as evidence.

Furthermore, when observing the enduring models established by these masters, it is truly difficult to fathom them through mere conjecture. Xuefeng was a spiritual teacher (kalyāṇamitra) of fifteen hundred people;

nine times he bit the finger at the butcher’s gate, yet Yunju was his "Wondrous Light" and "Illusory Existence. This great master of seven lifetimes in this land cast himself back into the furnace and forge to request the hammer—how much more so for those who were even more formidable?

Now that the artisan has passed away, [the tradition] is lost. *Note: The final character "操" (cāo) appears to be a fragment or an incomplete term, likely referring to the loss of the "craftsman's manual" or the "artisan's practice" (匠民).*
The axe loses its grip; the Sea-Seal (Haiyin) sinks its radiance. If one does not master the skill of pressing the finger, then for a month one will fail to glimpse the truth.
If the single source is not restored, then the nine streams will branch out in confusion, leading to the delusion of divergent paths.

That these paths are not unified while the finger is not forgotten is the concern of the true guide. This is why Caoshan [said]: [...]* *Note: The original text fragment ends abruptly. The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the quote from Caoshan.*
Various annotations were provided without reserve. Xía compiled them and Huī commented upon them;
this is how the present record came into circulation. However, as the phrasing is convoluted, it is somewhat difficult to investigate.

Recently, the Chan Master Lǎoqiān of Fǎpǔ obtained a Song edition and republished it, further collecting the lost writings of the Cáo-dòng lineage along with the discourses of the two masters Shūsān and Mòshān.

The *Juepai* (Arrangement of Decisions) was made into the lower fascicle. [I] lamented that it was not sufficiently detailed; consequently, there were many errors and contradictions, which constituted no small loss. I have often harbored this regret in my heart.
Once, when I visited Master Xiaorong of Caoxi and mentioned the lineage of the Cao-Dong school, the Master also expressed deep sighs of lamentation regarding this matter more than twice.
However, I did not have the leisure to inquire further into the details; now I am like one who bites his own heel in vain.
It has come to pass. In my heart, I have privately considered that I have encountered a fortunate karmic condition and must rectify my mind.
However, as the world is beset by many difficulties, I have not yet fulfilled my original aspirations. In the summer of the Bingchen year, I took up residence at Jixiang Hermitage on Lunsan Mountain.

Taking advantage of some leisure time, I took the old texts of the three masters’ discourses and, for the sake of easy consultation, rearranged their phrasing; I interspersed them according to the respective sections, following the original divisions.
It has been compiled into two volumes to satisfy the inquiries of the young and ignorant. Fellow practitioners and seniors who have long observed this work feared that the draft might perish;
thus, they earnestly requested its publication through carving blocks. I replied, "Excellent! May we rely upon the clarity of the Dharma-water to thoroughly wash away the dense growth of afflictions.
You should proceed with this plan. The term "Yuanjian" (Selected) refers to the words of Caoshan. As for the term "Shi" (Explanation)...

This is the Hu-language. As for the differences in detail and brevity between the two versions of the text, I have retained the detailed portions and omitted the brief ones. Where both versions are consistent, I have preserved both.
However, that the textual order varies does not imply any personal bias on my part. Regarding places where notes were missing or left unexplained, I have supplemented them with my limited knowledge.
For instance, in Zhi Mindu’s *Combined Text of the Śūraṅgama* and Du Kang’s *Interleaved Commentary on the Jiaoling*, how could such works have been lost?

The text is complete; though it is but a half-moon, its traces are imitated, and even a drop of dust is sufficient to fill a valley. It is my hope that by following the stream one may find the source, and by scooping from the sea one may recognize the river.
Thus, the Elder of Xinfeng shall avoid falling to the ground.

Preface to the *Five Ranks of Dongshan: The Revealed Instructions*, together with the *Essential Selections of the Former Caoshan*, compiled by the late Master Huixian of Yifeng Xiaoxuan on the eighth day of the month of Shishen in the first year of Zhongtong.
Recorded by his disciple, the Later Caoshan, Grand Master Liaowu, Huixia.
The Western Patriarch brought the flower, severing names and forms within the single truth; Master Nanhua went forth with the fruit, dispersing the five petals of the lineage transmission.
Reaching Xinfeng, he broadly upheld the essential principles; his single phrase of perfect fusion was divided into five sections.
Subsequently, the Great Master Caoshan, the direct successor of Xinfeng, sought to clarify the five ranks and produced five verses, while simultaneously citing an illustrative example.
These words serve to reveal the essential meaning of the five gates: first, the primary position acts as the host; second, the secondary position acts as the guest;
third, returning from the primary to the secondary is thus coming, which reveals the positions;

fourth, returning from the secondary to the primary is thus going, which clarifies the fundamental principle (*zong*); and fifth, bringing these together simultaneously, they do not involve existence or non-existence, and are suddenly extinguished.
Host and guest: neither biased nor partial, most wondrous and most profound. Sometimes they come head-on; how could one follow mere speech or silence?

Sometimes they depart face-to-face; how could this reside in verbal explanation? Like Yaoshan wearing a sword or Puna washing a Buddha—these are utterly beyond the rules of the teachings and stand out as a marvelous faculty outside the conventional.
Truly departing from the common path and completely transcending divergent ways, let us forever contemplate the essence of the School.
The purport is this: this stage is most profound. There are those who clarify its function by borrowing from the stage, and those who clarify the stage by preparing its function;

they distinguish the correct through conditions and realize the ultimate return through the wondrous essence. Even the most abstruse discourses all designate the sequence of stages. Having thus examined these essential points, I venture to compose this preface.
A Re-collated Collection of Dongshan’s Five Ranks of Bias and Rectitude and Caoshan’s Discerning Words, with Preface, composed by the disciple Guanghui. The preface states:
How extraordinary it is that the World-Honored One, within the ineffable Dharma, was able to establish all dharmas through verbal expression!
This is the gateway of skillful means for the teachings spoken by the Perfected One (Tathāgata). Generations of successors have looked up to this lofty mountain with reverence.

As for the Five Ranks of Bias and Rectitude (*piānzhèng wèiwèi*), these were composed by the Great Master of Dongshan. This Master was a sovereign physician of the Dharma-realm and a transformative being of the Chan school;
every one of his words and phrases penetrates the marrow and the spirit. He briefly opened the gate of skillful means.
In this gateway, he established the positions of the partial and the correct; his words were concise, yet their principles were profound. Heaven was not high, nor was the sea vast;
yet had one not entered the patriarch’s chamber, who could fathom its boundaries? Next was the Great Master Cao Shan, a man of the New School.
Having early on mastered the True Principle and further encountered an enlightened teacher, he received the texts directly from him and secretly transmitted the essential meaning. Not...
Fearing that the Way of the Teacher might decline, he presented this to his disciples. For those of superior intelligence, a single corner of it is easily understood;
for those of mediocre capacity, even after three repetitions, it remains difficult to clarify. Thereupon, he composed verses and arranged chapters as if obtaining divine jewels from the sea;

his word-by-word explanation was like gazing into a bright mirror to see one's own reflection. This is what is meant by "the father initiates the work and the son assists in its completion. Thus, it began:
Those who provide definitive explanations differ from day to day; those who depart full and arrive hungry knock at the gate not just once.
Selections are made according to priority, and thus words become increasingly redundant and complex. If one knows the pivotal gateway, the direct path is easily traversed.

Failing to reach the essential meaning of the fundamental principles, one remains long lost amidst words and phrases. Having traveled extensively between the North and South for over twenty years in search of instruction, I have frequently consulted teachers and friends regarding the True Doctrine.
Suddenly, upon encountering texts concerning the "partial" and the "correct," I began to somewhat discern the traces left by the ancients.
These are indeed the talking points of the Mysterious Gate and serve as a lamp in a dark room; yet, they were intended for the specific capacities of enlightened masters.

This abbreviated presentation is intended to provide a general overview by citing a single corner of the subject; those among the learned who have long studied it will surely understand its essential pivot.
However, there may be those of later generations who do not comprehend its ultimate intent; therefore, I have recorded the various schools in full to further set forth my own humble views.
Written by the long-time practitioner, the monk Mingxi (明夕). Should there be any errors, I pray that you will deign to provide your masterful correction. Thus it is said.

The supplement states: Shanqing said, "When Yanguan Jia first resided at Xinfeng and later moved to Dongshan, he greatly propagated his Way and established [the teaching]."
The Five Ranks of Bias and Orthodoxy (*wèi*) were the first to be proclaimed at that time; this is now also called the "Revealed Instructions of Dongshan.
Thus, it is a universal consensus that the establishment of the five ranks originated with Dongshan.
Consequently, the *Treasure Mirror Samādhi Song*, the *Inscription on the Profundities*, the *Snow Child Verse*, and the three verses on the "Essential Principles" share much of the same terminology.

All of these emerge from the realization of the fundamental source and are free from doubt. However, the *Sengbao zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha) states that when Caoshan wished to take his leave of Dongshan, Dongshan said, "Come at the third watch;
I shall instruct you in the details. When midnight arrived, [Dongshan] bestowed upon him the *Baoming sanmei* (Treasure Mirror Samādhi), the *Wuwei xianjue* (Five Ranks:
Revealed Instructions), and the *San shenlou* (Three Leaks), which had previously been entrusted to Yunyan. Furthermore, he offered this eulogy: "The Treasure Mirror Samādhi..."
The wording of these verses is essential and subtle. Yunyan transmitted them to Dongshan, who suspected they were the work of Yaoshan.

Because the former masters feared their widespread dissemination, they mostly kept them as precious secrets; however, the "Five Ranks" verses and the phrases regarding the "Three Leaks" appear in the Chan records.

Based on this, it seems that the *Samādhi-xianjue* (Exposition of the Secret Instructions on Samādhi), the verses for each rank, and the texts concerning the three leaks all originated from [Yaoshan].
Yaoshan was different from this; by what standard is the correct one to be determined?

Now, observing this through a narrow tube, I see that while the principles of the *Baojing xianjue* (The Precious Mirror’s Revealed Instructions) regarding the three outflows were all received from Yaofeng, as for the composition of texts, the establishment of positions, and their dissemination within the monastic community, these originated with Dongshan.
Therefore, the world refers to them as the "Dongshan Five Ranks. Furthermore, he personally inherited [the lineage] from Ke...
The Master Cao Shan and his disciples all stated that this was the revealed instruction (xianjue) of Dongshan; this serves as clear evidence.
Why must one be perplexed by later accounts? It is simply that the patriarchs kept it secret, fearing it would become widely disseminated.

Dongshan, however, threw open the doors and windows, and without any hesitation regarding the fundamental Dharma, he established its name and position and provided its practical application. Therefore, it is called "revealed" (xian).

The essential meaning can be understood from this. Some say that the *Pao-ching San-mei* (Treasure Mirror Samādhi) was composed by Yaoshan, while the rest were recounted through the lineage of Dongshan;
thus, the father established the foundation and the son completed the structure, nearly reaching perfection. However, within the school of Yaoshan there were two lineages:
one descending from Daowu down to Shishuang and Moshan (who is also known as Jiufeng), which for the most part followed the [former] path.

My father and I employed this [method]. From Yunyan down to the Cao-Dong lineage, masters have for the most part employed the "partial" and the "correct," while simultaneously encompassing the "ruler" and the "father.

Had Yaoshan already possessed the teachings on the "interchange of the correct and the partial" and the "three and five" within the *Baoming Sanmei* (Treasure Mirror Samādhi), he would have kept them secret and not transmitted them;
instead, he would have transmitted them privately only to Cheng. However, he did not do so.
The family traditions differ so greatly; why is this? Furthermore, it is questionable that Dongshan should have received the credit for being the first to initiate [this teaching].
Thus, regarding the composition of the *Baoying*, one may simply set aside what is uncertain.

As for the three "leaks" (*san shen lou*) in the *Xian jue*, these are clearly the instructions of Wuben, as evidenced by the *Tan zhang*. Within the *Baofeng zhuan*, the phrasing is somewhat vague and leads to...
He gave rise to doubt and hesitation. It is a pity.
That the position of correctness (zhèngwèi) is nonetheless partial (piān), yet can be discerned within the partial—this contains two meanings of "perfection" (yuán).

Caoshan selected [the meaning] and said: "The position of correctness is nonetheless partial" because it does not face objects. Although it does not face objects, objects are nonetheless fully present.
Huiguang’s commentary says: "Yet possessing" means possessing function. The distinction regarding "another time" states: that which is without function in the midst of the center is partial;
total function is perfect. These are two meanings. Question: What is meant by "total"? Answer: "One who does not look back" refers to one who has attained the ground.
This is because the state of the correct position (zhengwei) has not yet been clarified. Whether a Buddha appears in the world or not, it is just so. Whether a Buddha...
It does not emerge from the world; it is thus. Therefore, the thousands and ten-thousands of sages all return to the correct position to assume their responsibility.
The commentary states: "Not looking back" clarifies that one possesses the perfect function. Furthermore, regarding the two meanings of discerning the perfect within the partial:
because one discerns the correct position within the partial, it is called "total. Because one discerns its correct position within the partial, [it is so].

It is said to be "perfectly round. Each position of the biased and the correct possesses both meanings; since the biased and the correct are both perfectly round and both essence and function are fully present, it is called "two meanings.
Whenever there are words and phrases involving conditions, they are termed "function. Furthermore, to distinguish this specifically:

regarding the biased, the correct, and the simultaneous inclusion (jiandai) elucidated by our former masters, one should follow the original intent of those former masters and not treat them as a mere display of skill.
The stages of progressive cultivation involve both doctrinal formulations and direct, extraordinary discourse on the profound and wondrous essence.
This simply clarifies that the reality of the ancestors is manifest before us, in silent accord with the Way of the ancient sages.

Now, observing how various scholars interpret and select from the intentions of the former masters, it appears there may be some errors in their exposition. Unable to remain silent, I shall briefly set forth these discrepancies; I am deeply ashamed to do so.
Do not confuse their respective functions. Within this, there may be instances where the position is used to clarify the function, or the function is used to clarify the position;

the threads of these conditions are manifold, and the function depends on the occasion. One must observe the momentum of the words as they emerge and respond without failing the incoming opportunity; the subtlety lies simply in such exquisite refinement.

Supplement: I once examined the *Guang hongming ji* (Collection for the Propagation and Clarification of Buddhism). In the lecture halls, all members of the Śākya clan were addressed as "Scholars" (*xueshi*).

One monk was planting upside down. Dongshan asked, "Reverend, why are you planting upside down? He replied, "Because my mind is alive. The Master did not say anything and returned to the monastery.
The next day, when the assembly of monks went out for communal labor, he went out first to wait and ask about the one who had planted upside down yesterday.
A monk who had been working in the fields came out. As the monk was leaving through the gate, Master Shan asked him, "Venerable sir, who was it that cut the bamboo in the eastern garden yesterday?
The monk, not knowing what he meant, replied, "I do not know. Shan asked, "Where are you from, Venerable sir?"
It is said that he was a man from Dengzhou. Mount Shandao remarked, "When I was traveling as a wandering monk, I once went there.
Furthermore, while the assembly at Mount Wuyue were working in the fields, Shandao went out intending to join them at the site of the work. He happened to encounter Yangshan coming up from the field.
Shandao asked, "How many people are in the field? Yangshan then thrust his spade into the ground and stood leaning against it. Shandao—
It is said, "Today many people on the South Mountain are harvesting thatch. Instances of such language are not commonly used;

examine them closely. Jian said: "For example, when the Scholar Jian spoke of 'detaching alone from the mundane world and arising before all sages,' he said, 'This is the true position, yet it is perfectly round.
In reality, this is a bending of the true position. Such examples of language were spoken by the ancients."
The traces of this [error] still remain; one has not yet attained "no words within words. This is further called "not being in the true position" (*asamyaktva-sthāna*).
Because there are "words within words," it may be called "having an illness accompanied by a trace," but it must not be called "the state of mutual accompaniment.
The commentary states: These are the words of Master Cao Shan disparaging the Venerable Zhen. If they were not...
Profoundly attuned to the mysterious pivot, who would dare to distinguish its orthodoxy or heterodoxy? A single word of praise or censure serves as an illuminating standard for ten thousand ages.
Regarding those who speak of being uniquely liberated beyond the mundane world, it is said in the discourse of Master Sengzhao: "Principle is governed by the spirit;
it alone shines brilliantly before all the sages. Baizhang said: "My words concerning being uniquely liberated beyond the mundane world arise from before the assembly of the sages."
Yunyan then raised this statement, saying: "I say it is solitary liberation beyond all things; how could it be before the various sages?
These words were Yunyan’s way of assisting and clarifying the Director’s (Tiju) remark; thus, the two characters "how" (qǐ) and "could" (kě) each have their own underlying significance.
The meaning that those who study Dark Learning (Xuánxué) must understand. [Supplement]: The name "right position" (*zhèngwèi*) is not restricted to the Dòngshàng school;
it originates from the teachings of the Vehicle itself. As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states:

"If those who hear this teaching have not yet entered the right position and eat this food, they will only be able to digest it after entering the right position. Those who have already entered the right position and eat this food..."
It is only after attaining liberation of mind that [the afflictions] are then eliminated. The "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokadhātuparivarta*) in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:
"The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva takes all emptiness as his dwelling place because he skillfully observes it;

he takes the signless (*animitta*) as his dwelling place because he does not depart from the state of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and so forth. The *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "This is the perfuming of essence and function (*tathatā-vāsanā*)."
There are two kinds (and so forth). The *Śāstra* says: "The first are those who have not yet entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*);

the second are those who have already entered the stage of certainty. What are those who have not yet entered the stage of certainty? This refers to ordinary beings of the ten stages of faith, all followers of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness.

Because they have not attained the wisdom of the true essence (*samyag-mūla-jñāna*) and have not realized suchness as it truly is, they remain as they were originally. First, [they are] those whose characteristics have not yet manifested.

It is so. This refers to ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, who practice by means of the perfuming of the mental consciousness and through the power of faith.

Because they have not yet attained a non-conceptual mind that accords with the essence [of reality], and because they have not yet attained mastery over karma such that their practice accords with its function, how can they be said to have entered the stage of certainty? It is said to be the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The Bodhisattva attains the wisdom of the fundamental nature internally and the subsequently attained wisdom externally. In one respect, their application of wisdom is equal to that of a Tathāgata;

they naturally cultivate practice through the power of original perfuming, increase True Suchness (*tathatā*), and are able to extinguish ignorance, thereby returning to the original state—this is the first [stage of] "already being in correspondence.
This refers to Dharma-body Bodhisattvas who have attained non-conceptual mind and, together with all...
The functioning of Buddha-wisdom corresponds [to this]: relying solely on the power of the Dharma, one naturally practices, perfuming True Suchness (tathatā) and thereby extinguishing ignorance.
Thus, Master Yantou said: "A single power resides in the place of turning; it is like a gourd upon ice, drifting aimlessly at ease.
If you press down on it, it turns. If it were to come from within the state of the Correct Position (zhengwei), it would not be so."
He dresses it up with elaborate patterns and garnishes; when he calls this "not thinking of a single thing," it is also called the "right phrase" (*zhengju*).
It is also called "profound stillness" (*zhan-zhan-di*), also called the "solitary peak," and also called the "crown king."

Although the state of partiality is indeed partial, it also possesses the two meanings of perfection; this is distinguished within the context of conditions. It is "having words" while being "without words. To clarify:
because it is not established for the sake of utility, that which is not established is the Real, and thus it is not something used conventionally. The commentary states:

"Although the state of partiality is indeed partial, it also possesses the two meanings of perfection, because it is distinguished within the context of conditions; this is 'having words' within [the state of] existence."
It is wordless because its function does not abide in anything established. That which does not abide in anything established is true; it cannot be used as a conventional constant.
Because both the biased and the correct are manifested together, it is called the "perfect duality.

Furthermore, that "there is wordlessness within words" when discerned within conditions means that while engaging with conditions, one clarifies the subtle mystery; by borrowing phrases, the essence is revealed. Moreover, its function does not abide in anything established.

Although this is explained from the perspective of function, it does not contradict the perspective of words. Furthermore, it is distinguished by saying: "Though the position of partiality is partial, it is also complete.

This refers to two meanings: that within function there is nothing to which one does not touch. Although this is explained from the perspective of function, it does not contradict the perspective of words.
This is like saying "as it is" all day long while not actually saying anything. It is also said: "The position of partiality is, in fact, complete."

"Furthermore, it is endowed with non-contact within conditions. The commentary explains: "Regarding the two meanings of 'no object within function' and 'non-contact,' this refers to the non-contact between the two intentions of guest and host.
Dongshan asked a monk, "What is your name? The monk replied, "Please, Master, bestow a name upon me.

How [should one respond]? Daowu said, "Come along with me. Furthermore, someone asked Yunju, "What is the meaning of 'come along with me'?

At midnight, the Wood Child knocks at the moon-gate, Startling the Jade Woman from her sleep in the dark.
Deviant within the Centered: Sea clouds linger atop the sacred mountain peaks; The traveler returns to find his hair turned white and hanging low.
Silk [threads]—ashamed to face the cold reflection on the Terrace of Qin, arriving from the very center.
On a moonlit night, the long *gong* dragon sheds its shell and opens it; its great back rubs the heavens as it shakes its cloud-feathers.
Its soaring and roaming through the Bird Path are difficult to describe.
Simultaneous Arrival: Meeting face-to-face, there is no need for mutual avoidance; The subtle meaning of unimpaired transformation is within the light.
A path exists naturally within that light, distinct from the ordinary.
Simultaneous Reaching: The handle of the Dipper hangs slantwise as the sky has not yet dawned; The crane’s dream has just awakened amidst the misty dew.
Cold. The old nest flies out; the cloud-pines have fallen.
Again, a small *can* (private instruction). A monk asked, "What is 'the biased within the central'? The Master said, "The sky dawns with white clouds. "What is 'the central within the biased'?
The Master said, "The water flows with the bright moon. "What is 'coming from the central'? The Master said, "Do not..."
The Way is like the *kūn* and *jīng* fish, which have no wings; today I have personally returned by the path of birds. What is "reaching within the partial"? The Master said:

"When the occasion arises, there is no mutual exchange; face-to-face, there is neither before nor after. What is "arriving within the inclusive"? The Master said: "In the jeweled palace, there is no one who does not stand in attendance;
if one does not plant the *wútóng* tree, the phoenix will not come. I have already received the Master’s instruction on these five ranks.
"Is there anything further beyond this? The Master said, "There is. "What is that which is beyond? The Master said, "It would be better to cut out one's tongue;
who would dare to face it head-on?"
Miaoxi addressed the assembly, saying:
"Furthermore, there is another kind [of teaching] that takes the mutual interplay of the partial and the whole as its fundamental principle.

It uses black and white circles to represent the formal characteristics of the five ranks (*wuwei*). It takes the entirely black circle as representing the state before Vipaśyin Buddha and before one's parents were born."
The state prior to the emergence of the kalpa of birth, when the primordial chaos had not yet been divided, is called the "Correct Position" (*zhengwei*).

Representing this by means of a circle that is two parts black and one part white is termed "Centered Deviation" (*zhengzhongpian*). One must then come from the white portion to speak of the black, yet one must not violate the character for "black";
to violate the character for "black" would be to touch upon a taboo. Furthermore, he cites a verse by Dongshan: "Centered Deviation: the third watch..."
"Before the moonlight of the first watch": this means one can employ a shift in expression by speaking only of the "third watch.

The third watch is dark; the first watch is dark; and the period before the moonlight is dark. By not saying "dark" but instead saying "the third watch," "the first watch," or "before the moonlight," one employs a shift in expression that avoids touching upon taboos.
Taking two parts white and one part black as a circle represents "centered within the partial"; yet it comes back [to the whole].
To speak of white upon a black ground, yet not to touch upon the news of the white ground itself. The verse says: "Correctness within the partial;
an elderly woman at dawn encounters an ancient mirror. It does not speak of brightness or whiteness, but rather of "dawn" and an "ancient mirror.

This is the ability to employ *huìhù* (reciprocal avoidance) regarding the characters for "brightness" and "white" so as not to touch upon taboos. For "dawn" is the brightness within darkness, and the "ancient mirror" [is the clarity within obscurity].
This is also clarity within darkness. Although the old woman’s hair is white, she does not say "white" but says "old woman";

the word "white" is already contained therein, for she is able to employ the term "white" with intentional ambiguity (*huìhù*). Furthermore, he speaks of "coming from the very center. The verse says: "Coming from the very center;

there is a path within the midst, yet it is obscured by dust. Some say it should read "emerging from the dust," meaning that whenever there are words or phrases, they are all sung from the midst of the non-existent.
Upon emerging, one spontaneously grasps the wondrous understanding; there is nothing that does not come from within the state of right position (*samyaktva*).

Whether manifest or obscure, whether arriving or reaching, all are instances of grasping and penetrating the fundamental source. Every single stage (*bhūmi*) possesses these five matters, just as a hand possesses its five fingers.
"Neither lacking nor excessive; it arrives within the inclusive. This means arriving by being inclusive of both black and white, and inclusive of both the partial and the correct.

What is meant by "arriving"? It is like a person returning home who has already arrived even before reaching the destination. Other activities are merely matters on the road for those at the periphery;

yet these too can be interchanged. The subtlety lies in what precedes the essence. "Arriving within the inclusive" means that all four preceding positions are embraced by the subtle and thus return [to the source].

The "Correct Position" (zhengwei) is described as "returning to the fold and sitting amidst the charcoal. This also refers to the dark realm (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*), where the character for "black" is replaced by its homophone for "charcoal.
One does not say "black," but rather speaks of "charcoal. Furthermore, it is said that Caoshan stated: "The Correct Position is the realm of emptiness;
it is entirely devoid of things. The Partial Position is the realm of form; within it are all manner of diverse and myriad phenomena."

As for "Manifesting the Image" (*xiàng*): that which "reaches both simultaneously" (*jiānzhōng zhì*) abandons phenomena to enter into principle; that which "comes from within the Middle Way" (*zhèngzhōng lái*) turns away from principle to attend to phenomena.
That which "carries both together" (*jiāndài*) is the silent response to all conditions without falling into any state of existence; it is neither defiled nor pure, neither correct nor biased.

Therefore, it is called the "Vast and Mysterious Essential Path," the "Unattached True Doctrine. The former masters of antiquity have deduced that this single position is the most wondrous and the most profound. One must...
This is a careful and detailed examination of the essential nature [of the teaching]. Furthermore, it is said that each of the five stages consists of three characters forming a sentence;

through the mutual interplay of the biased and the correct, the upper and the lower, one does not err against the center. The "center" is precisely the position of correctness (*zhengwei*). There are explicit clarifications in the teachings regarding both the explanation of principle (*li*) and the explanation of phenomena (*shi*).
Is the Way of the direct pointing transmitted outside the teachings truly like this? If it is indeed like this, then what is so wonderful about Caoshan?
This is merely a tangle of oral transmission and mental instruction. Since it is not thus, what was the ultimate intention of the ancients?
Miaoxi shall provide a commentary for you, so that those everywhere may examine it.
Have you not seen Fengyang say: "The face and features are manifest before you; choose whichever you will"? Therefore, Vimalakīrti said: "Simply remove the illness, but do not remove..."
The Dharma. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If you listen to the Dharma with a mind of conditions, this Dharma is also a condition.
Although the single words and half-phrases of the ancients were expressions of compassion, they all reached [the listener] before one had even defecated. Master Jinsi said:

"The position of correctness, the position of partiality, coming from within correctness, arriving from within partiality, and reaching through the integration of both. Based on what has been stated above, each possesses its own skillful means (*upāya*).
The Elder Yuanzhen selected and supplemented [the text], saying:
"This selection has already been rejected by Caoshan. However, people today do not know the full beginning and end of the matter; moreover—"
It is not without merit; therefore, the ancient editions have recorded it as well. The essential point is to distinguish between gain and loss.

Although the "correct position" (zhengwei) is actually "partial" (pian), it also contains the two meanings of "perfect" (yuan). When one asks about that which has not yet arisen, it is called "partial.

At such a time, when no one can provoke or disturb it, these two meanings are called "perfect. It is also called the "Master within the Master. As Yunyan said: "It is solitary and detached from all things."
Externally, it arises before all the sages.

Although its partiality has two meanings, within this speech there is no speech; the mere presence of words is partiality, yet even in that partiality, there is no speech within the speech—this is the second meaning.
It is also called the "host within the guest. For example, as when asking about Luzu.
Exhalation does not depend on various conditions; inhalation does not abide within the aggregates or elements. What is the meaning of this? The Patriarch said:
"There is one person who has neither exhalation nor inhalation. This answer is a statement that differs from the literal expression.
Furthermore, because the questioner’s perspective was partial, the answer corresponds directly to the actual state; therefore, it is called "perfect" (yuan).
There are those who come from within the state of correct positioning (*samyaktva*). Within silence there is speech; they are asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch?
and they reply, "Wait until the hornless ox (*viṣāṇa*) gives birth to a calf, and then I shall tell you. They further say, "When you had not yet asked, I remembered it;
as soon as you asked, I have forgotten. This is speech within silence. Although this speech is primary...
The *Jiayu* (Family Sayings) is also used by both guest and host; it is also called "the host within the host. [A guest] asks: "I intend to ask such-and-such, but when I try to speak it, I cannot.
What do you say? [The host] replies: "I also cannot speak it. This constitutes the complete fulfillment of both host and guest. It is like Dongshan’s question to Yunyan:
"Before the realms of form and shadow existed, could one still say 'it is' or 'it is not'? Yunyan said: "Do you have it now? These words are for the purpose of [pointing to] non-existence.

Within words there are words. Sometimes there are those that come from a partial standpoint; sometimes there are words within which there are no words. [A question was asked: "What is the profound principle? [The reply was:
"It is like the tongue of a dead man. Again [a question was asked: "What thing comes in such a way? [The reply was: "To describe it as a single thing is immediately inadequate. This.
This is shared by both host and guest; it is also called "the master among guests. Furthermore, there are expressions of merit that contain no words.
For instance, when asked, "What do you offer throughout the twelve hours? he replied, "Nothing. Or, as when asked of Dongshan, "Where have the former sages gone now?
the Master said, "They have gone to a place beyond pursuit. This response within the dialogue seems to come from the side of merit. Therefore...
It is said that within speech there is no speech; in reality, this is not a matter of deliberate achievement. This speech comes alone, and for this reason it is called "partial.
Alternatively, there may be instances where things arrive together; here, one must first attain non-delusion. Question:

When light and objects both vanish, what is it then? Answer: It is perfectly clear and distinct. If you can discern it at the moment it arises, this is also called "discerning the host within the guest."
There are also cases where [the guest] arrives accompanied by other causes and conditions; it is not necessarily the case that they come from within the "correct position" (*zhengwei*).

Furthermore, regarding those who come from the "partial position" (*piānwei*), although among the speech of those who arrive together there may be distinctions between the "master of masters" and the "master of guests," or between the intimate and the distant, these still belong to the partial position and are likewise peripheral remarks.
If, at the moment of arrival, someone urgently summons [a guest], one should extract them and bring them back [to the main assembly].
Regarding the fundamental position: Baizhang also said, "Set aside the throat, lips, and mouth, and bring forth a single phrase. A student said, "I cannot say it;
please let the Master say it. The Master said, "I do not refuse to speak for you, but I fear that later generations might deceive my descendants."

Yunyan asked, "Does the Master still have any [of this] now? The Master replied, "I have lost my descendants. Again, when asked about Dongshan, [the Master said], "I received from the Abbot the teaching of 'scraping-bone Chan.
I request the Abbot to scrape it from all four directions and eight sides. [Dongshan] replied, "There is no place to scrape."
The monk said, "Master, you are fortunately a skilled hand; why then can you not cure me? The Master said, "Listen then:
the world’s physicians fold their hands. This question was compounded with a secondary element; therefore, the answer directly manifested the matter at hand.
Thus, both question and answer failed to touch upon [the ultimate reality], which is why it is said they were brought together as a compound.
Generally speaking, the rhetorical dynamics between the questioner and the respondent in these two cases do not exceed two underlying meanings.

In both instances, the questions vary in their coarseness or subtlety, while the answers differ in their depth or shallowness. This is why my late teacher Dongshan forcefully employed words within a state that transcends language;
this is a wondrous principle established to respond to conditions through skillful means, intended to eliminate doubts and dispel delusions for those of future generations.
Discerning the heterodox to distinguish the orthodox, knowing the proper order of host and guest, one masters the two extremes of partiality and correctness.

As for the five ranks (*wuwei*), they were specifically established by Master Dongshan in his interactions with sentient beings.

Although they belong to the realm of verbal teaching, for the most part they do not exceed these five ranks. As for the subtle and profound meaning—those who ascend to the hall of Dongshan and enter the chamber of Dongshan, it was only Caoshan.
The Master knew he was destined for this; he was indeed a numinous being from the realm of Śakra. Thus...
I append this in the form of a verse on the five ranks. Cao Shan treasured it; even a foot-long jade disc or an inch of gold is not to be compared to its value.
I have composed this specifically for later students, citing the essential teachings of the former masters to provide proof. Cao Shan alone examined it and scrutinized it with precision;
all others merely cling to one-sided views, falling into conceptualization and mental fabrication. You, my wise and discerning friends, should examine this with careful attention.
As for those who were indolent and base, they spoke according to their own convenience; five thousand people rose from their mats and departed.
The Great Master did not restrain them, for even such a withdrawal is excellent. Within this school’s ultimate purpose, one rarely encounters a single person in the course of a month or a year.

I, an uninitiated junior student, have had the honor of being in close proximity to my late mentor. Having inherited from afar the instructions he bestowed upon me, I have observed that those who mistakenly grasp this meaning each give rise to their own biased interpretations;
this has constantly pained the very marrow of my bones, and I can no longer restrain myself. Thus, I shall briefly set forth the essential points.
This is designated as the "Five Ranks" (*Wuwei Baokhe Lun*).
"The Centered Bias" (*Zhengzhongpian*) refers to the Master among masters. It simply does not involve external conditions; it is a turning about that does not touch anything else.
One attains the Way within phenomena, like discerning [colors] before black and white have been distinguished. This is the Master among masters, not the Master among guests.
The primary subject within the guests is speechless when facing conditions, while there is speech within the midst of non-speech; this is "the partial within the central" (zheng zhong pian).

When one realizes attainment through this very partiality, it is called "the primary subject within the primary subject" (zhu zhong zhu). Therefore, all that is perfect is merely the turning of these peripheral things, which wondrously contain its principle.
"They do not touch one another. Thus the Great Master’s verse says: "The partial within the absolute; the third watch of the night, before the bright moon. Caoshan explained this, saying:
"When black and white are not yet distinguished, if one can discern [this], one does not involve oneself with conditions.

But if one discerns it when black and white have already been distinguished, this is not the 'Master within the Master'; rather, involving oneself with conditions is being the 'Master within the Guest. This is called..."

Distinguishing the host within the guest: "Do not be surprised that we meet yet do not recognize one another; hidden away, I still cherish my former elegance. Cao Shan selected this saying and remarked:
"Although this phrase is close, it is not identical. It is the 'host within the host' because it does not face conditions (*pratyaya*).

If it were identical, it would face them; thus it is the 'host within the guest. Although it faces conditions, its functioning is not the same. As Yunyan said: 'It stands alone, detached from all things.'"
Externally, how could it be before the assembly of sages? It is just as it was before there were any sages; is this not clearly an analogy for when black and white have not yet been distinguished?
Cao Shan said, "Consider it most profoundly: it is also like when a black bean has not yet sprouted.
There are many such analogies; I have briefly cited the general outline.
Supplement: Throughout this discourse, the frequent mention of "serving the superior" refers to the "wondrous embrace within the center.

"Entering the center from the partial" clarifies that while engaging with conditions, one’s merit is not uniform; it is to discern, from within words, that which is beyond words, and thus it is perfectly round.
Although one enters through various gateways, it is not as if one enters from the outside; for it proceeds from a single word.

The following clarifies this attainment: although it involves a slight degree of conditions, it differs from ordinary conditions. For example, when a layman is appointed as a high minister, that is merely a matter of various conditions.
However, when one delivers a final verdict today, the engagement with conditions becomes profound and wondrous. The Great Master said: "It is like a king requesting a precious vessel;
if it is struck once with a hammer, the seams and joints are severed at once. Must one then resort to a second blow? He replied, "No."
"Only after decapitating oneself can one then execute the nine clans. But how should one act? Shishuang said: "One day born, one day a king. It is also said:
"A single push requires a word to push it away. Your present moment belongs to conditions;
therefore, it is called 'conditions,' and as soon as you strike upon them, you pass directly to the other side. If you can take responsibility there, how could it belong to conditions? Therefore...
It is perfectly complete. It is like a crown prince born in the royal palace; from the moment of birth, he is already within the palace and does not enter from without.
It is like the mark of a seam severed by a single blow of a hammer: at the very moment the hammer is applied, the seam is severed through conditions;
how then could this belong to any deliberate effort? Nevertheless, one must not cling to this [realization], for it is not a vessel inherently possessed by the King. Thus it is said:
The Crown Prince was born in the royal palace; though he is of royal lineage, he is not yet a king. The Great Master’s verse says:
"Centered within the slant, the old woman who has lost her way at dawn returns to recognize her own shadow. Is this not precisely clinging to this very thing?

For while involvement with conditions begins from this day, one must realize that the Crown Prince in the palace cannot immediately be called a king. With a single blow, the seams and stitches are severed.
One must not recognize this as a vessel inherently possessed by the King. It is a single substance with two meanings; it is simply that the timing differs.

Unless one has personally attained the profound essence of Dongshan, any other approach will involve mere calculation and conceptualization. For example, when asked, "Great Master, what is the Buddha?
he replied, "Not a Buddha. This is because "Buddha" is a condition (*pratyaya*); since the point of inquiry arises from conditions, it is likewise [not the Buddha].
To turn toward you from conditions is not the Buddha; it cuts you off and sends you over to that other side.

There is a class of people who interpret this on the tip of their tongues, calling it "using a wedge to drive out a wedge. Though they may manage to eliminate the "Buddha," what can they do about the fact that it is still not the Buddha?
The late Master said that one must not stop there; one must not merely waste effort on empty phrases and names.
It is like being struck by a single hammer—only then can the seams and stitches be severed. One must not use a wedge to drive out another wedge.
When I say to you here that it is "not Buddha," I am pushing you toward that other side. But how will you take up that other side? It is a great difficulty, a great challenge.
Difficult! I urge you, my fellow students of later generations, to be most diligent and thorough. Do not be like a blind donkey walking blindly on its feet.
You must seek the realization that existed before all Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm had yet come into being.

If you can realize this point subtly and profoundly, you will naturally possess the capacity for discourse; ultimately, there will be no failure to understand the language. The Buddha did not require the study of idle talk.
Verse. A former master said: "If you only know that the mind is Buddha, where would Buddha not understand speech?

One who comes from the state of ultimate reality (the correct position) does so by following the momentum of speech. To call this "speech within the speechless" is to speak of it in terms of conventional phenomena.
However, if one merely follows this, one will not encounter it directly.
As for the "True Status" (Zhengwei), it is from this status that all Buddhas and sentient beings within the Dharma-realm flow forth, just as myriad bubbles arise from the sea.
It is only to respond to conditions that the True Status is pointed out indirectly. If one does not respond to conditions, what would you call it? Even the Dharmakāya Buddha...
"Belonging to conditions. Because it is subject to change, Nanquan said, "To call it 'Suchness' (tathatā) is already a change;

one must walk within the midst of the heterogeneous. He was asked, "What is the heterogeneous? He replied, "If I were to tell you, when would you ever attain the heterogeneous? It would take as long as a donkey's years!
He further said, "Within the heterogeneous, one should not conform to categories. Does he speak in this way because he is still involved with conditions? He also spoke of "black beans."
When the sprout had not yet emerged, Yaoshan said, "I have a single phrase that I have never spoken to anyone.
Daowu said, "It has followed me here. This is because it has come forth in perfect harmony with the words; thus he said, "It has followed me here.
Xuefeng said, "When you entered the gate, I already discussed it with you. Guishan said, "Why did you not ask the old monk about this sooner? This—
There are many such examples; I cannot cite them all at length. I urge my fellow students of later generations: first, you must clearly realize the Correct Position (*samyaktva*).
You must seek it prior to the existence of the Dharma-body Buddha, prior to the existence of empty space, and prior to the existence of the True Suchness Dharma-realm (*tathatā-dharmadhātu*).
Therein, you must take the Dharma-body to be light, Mahāprajñāpāramitā to be light, and Amitāyus to be light. One...
All sentient beings and the vajra-body are entirely light. But what kind of light is this? How do you understand it before the light has even arisen?
Light and light are all dependent on conditions; if one does not face conditions, how can the true state (zhengwei) be manifested?
It is like a nail driven into empty space. Nevertheless, even so, a master must have words. Thus, Dongshan’s verse says: "The True..."
It comes from within; there is no "within" that reaches the point of severing the tongue. It merely belongs to the exhaustion of conditions, which is but dust and grime.
A master simply has words by the side of this very point, skillfully grasping the essence; thus one does not suffer injury. If one suffers injury, the tongue is severed.
If one remains silent, it is as if being buried alive. Examine this carefully.
Supplement: Regarding the matter of "burying while alive," it likely draws upon the karmic conditions of Prince Mopò (Mūkaputra).

As for the phrase "arriving at the ultimate within the partial" (*piān zhōng zhì zhě*): because it contains the wondrous ultimate principle within its discourse, it does not cause injury; it is thus the "host within the guest."
"Directly in the center and yet biased" is the master within the masters. "Biased and yet directly in the center" is the master within the guests.

Coming from the position of directness is coming as one who is uniquely liberated; there is no question of guest or host. Reaching the state of being biased is likewise following alone from the biased;
it is a subtle harmony that does not touch [the other]. When masters meet, they are like two blades facing each other, establishing their very lives upon the edge of the sword. They do not...
It is contact. Within this, one must either be a master or lose one's life. Therefore, when masters meet, there can be no silence.
Thus the verse says: "Reaching within the partial; the two-edged blade reaches the heavens. Because the momentum of the speech does not follow the partial, it contains within it a state of no-speech.
It is clearly spoken with the full mouth, yet because no trace is left, there are no seams or gaps. From...
This transcends both extremes; therefore, it is also said that "within speech there is no speech. As Shishuang said: "Three dice have been cast and do not fall. Yongquan said:
"No one can reach his precarious point," and again: "He hangs not a single thread of silk. Shishuang said: "He has no inhalation or exhalation.
Yangshan said: "Two mouths have but one tongue. Instances such as these are very numerous.
Furthermore, that which is brought forth does not involve the two paths of the biased or the correct; this stage is like being in the midst of a mysterious path while there is no mysterious path.
It is because its verbal expression is entirely non-conceptual, resembling empty space; it cannot be grasped when presented, and thus it is the ultimate subtlety.
For example, when Yaoshan saw Zun Bunan washing a Buddha statue, he asked him: "This [statue] is being washed by you; can you wash it?"
"Have you attained that? [The monk] said, "Bring that here. The Master then desisted. Furthermore, when Yaoshan was carrying a sword, Daowu asked, "What is that behind you?
Yaoshan struck him across the mouth with it. Again, Daowu asked, "When you make offerings to the Arhats today, do they still come?
Yaoshan replied, "What do you eat every day? Such examples are very numerous.
This is called "simultaneously encompassing that which is entirely without the 'precise' (di-di). Now, is this very thing itself precise?
If it were precise, it would belong to the category of objective things. As the ancients said: "A thousand comparisons cannot reach it; ten thousand illustrations cannot suffice.
Nevertheless, one must not categorically deny that it is precise. Therefore, Dongshan’s verse says: "Arriving within the simultaneous encompassing..."
Having fallen into the embers, sit there. Furthermore, does anyone ultimately attain this wondrous state? Must you wait for it to be perfectly clear?
Examine this minutely; do not allow yourself to fall into conceptualization or intellectual speculation.

Generally speaking, one must not adhere dogmatically to a single perspective when interpreting the force of these expressions. For example, it is like saying, "Once the ox gives birth to its calf, I shall tell you.
Or again, it is like the path of birds in the sky; this cannot be distinguished by means of the five ranks (*wuwei*), for it comes from the way of the profound mystery (*xuanye*).
It is not the same as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare—this is indeed an ancient teaching. This very thing is like...
This is the most sublime of the sublime. It is neither like empty space nor like the moon reflected in water; it is, rather, a distinct category of wondrous discourse.
Within the teachings, an analogy is given: when a mani jewel is in the sky, it is clear; when it is in the human world, it is turbid.
If it is wrapped in the five colors, it appears as the five colors; if placed in water, it takes on the color of the water. Its essence is not the five colors.

This was likely because the ancients thoroughly understood the nature of things. As the Great Master Fu said: "It has never been absent for even a moment, yet its full manifestation is before one's eyes;
though it is thus manifest, it is difficult to pursue and difficult to seek. Furthermore, it is like the present World-Honored One’s awakening.

A verse on the Way says: "One attains awakening because of the stars; after awakening, it is not the stars. One does not follow after objects, yet it is not that there are no stars. The substance of things is wondrously so.

If you can understand this through these lines, you may gradually be able to cast yourself into the state of right position (*samyaktva*). Generally, people nowadays see only the realm of words and phenomena;
they only know how to seek the sprouts, but do not know how to discern from the root. It is only by receiving the root that one attains life.

Thus, blue and yellow differ; flowers and plants are manifold. This applies to categories such as the Buddha-nature, Prajñā, Nirvāṇa, and the Dharmakāya, as well as to birth-and-death, afflictions, sentient beings, and insentient things—each of these colors and forms is distinct.

Even regarding the teachings and their distributed meanings, whether profound or shallow, if one understands them by looking down from the root, then there is no sprout that will not be understood. It is like the saying from Zhonghe in Shu: [the branches follow the root].
Shangyun said: "If I were to exclusively proclaim the vehicle of the school (zongcheng), the paths within the Chouling mountains would surely fall into ruin.

This refers to the primary position (zhengwei). Yet, later students shun calling it the primary position; this is because they do not seek realization at the root, but instead exclusively pursue the mysterious understanding through the branches.
As Shishuang said: "He rejects the mind and intellect, and he detests talk of seeing and hearing. Up to this point...
Regarding the Buddha of the Dharma-body, this is seeing and hearing. This refers to entering the stage of correct realization after having cast away [delusions].

But as for being free from seeing and hearing—where would one arrive? Master Cen said: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time and all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm are the light of Mahāprajñā.
Before this light has arisen, how can one understand it? This is to clear away [delusions] from the very root.
This is a matter of great shock! How many people under the sun have ever attained such thorough penetration? Unless one attains clear and penetrating realization, it will be a great calamity.
I urge you all to investigate and resolve this with meticulous care. You must let out the lion’s roar; do not utter the howl of a jackal.
My repeated entreaty to you! My repeated entreaty to you!
